title: From the Poet's House to the Sacred Books: Dessau to Oxford
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Poet's House — Dessau and the Enchanted Island

stops.name: Dessau — the birth in the Ducal residence-town of Anhalt
stops.campa: On the sixth of December, in the little residence-town of Anhalt-Dessau, a son is born to Wilhelm Müller, the ducal librarian and famous poet, and to Adelheide, daughter of the chief minister von Basedow. The child is named Max after the hero of Weber's Freischütz, an opera just finished when he was born; Carl Maria von Weber himself stands godfather. Here, Müller will write, one lived 'as in an enchanted island.' Into a house of music and verse the future editor of the Veda is set down — the last, small kingdom of German Romanticism, from which he will one day carry the scriptures of Asia into English.
stops.quote: In a small town such as Dessau was when I lived there as a child and as a boy, one lived as in an enchanted island.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, My Autobiography: A Fragment (1901)

stops.name: Dessau — the father's death and the songs Schubert set
stops.campa: The father dies at three-and-thirty, worn out young; Max is scarcely four. He keeps of him only a memory of a bright and sunny man delighted with the children's naughtinesses. Wilhelm Müller had been the 'Greek-Müller,' whose Lieder der Griechen roused Germany for the Greeks against the Turk; and he had written two cycles of wanderer's songs, Die schöne Müllerin and Winterreise, which Franz Schubert set to music. The father's verse will outlive him in the mouths of singers; the son, left to a widowed mother of eight-and-twenty, will spend his life editing other men's sacred songs, the hymns of a people older than Greece.
stops.quote: Fremd bin ich eingezogen, / Fremd zieh' ich wieder aus. (A stranger I arrived, a stranger I depart.)
stops.quote_source: Wilhelm Müller, 'Gute Nacht,' Winterreise (set by Schubert, 1827)

segments.name: The Schools of Saxony — Leipzig and the Turn to Sanskrit

stops.name: Leipzig — the Nikolaischule and the poor scholar
stops.campa: At twelve the boy is sent to Leipzig and enters the Nicolai school, boarding in the house of Professor Carus. He has nothing to live on, he later writes, but the fingers with which he holds his pen. He is steeped in Greek and Latin, in the classics that are the whole education of a German gymnasiast, and in music, for which he shows real gift. The poet's son, portionless, learns early the discipline of the seat and the lamp — the copying, the memorizing, the exactness — that will one day let him collate a thousand pages of a Vedic manuscript without a slip.
stops.quote: I had nothing to depend on after I left the University, but those fingers with which I still hold my pen.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, My Autobiography: A Fragment (1901)

stops.name: Leipzig University — the doctorate on Spinoza, 1843
stops.campa: In 1841 he matriculates at the University of Leipzig, meaning to read philology and philosophy. In September 1843, not yet twenty, he takes his doctorate with a dissertation on the third book of Spinoza's Ethics. But already another current has caught him: in the lecture-rooms of Hermann Brockhaus he has met Sanskrit, the ancient sacred tongue of India, and the vast unedited hymnody that lies behind it. The Western classics have made him a scholar; the Eastern tongue will make him a discoverer. He resolves to give his life to the language and the literature of the Aryas.

stops.name: Leipzig — under Brockhaus, first Sanskrit and the Hitopadesa
stops.campa: Under Brockhaus he masters the Devanagari and reads the fables of the Hitopadesa, whose German translation he will soon publish — his first book. The letters of the sacred script, once learned, never leave him; he says a scholar must learn to read a manuscript as a musician reads a score. India opens before him as a second, older Greece, and he conceives the plan that will govern half a century: to print, for the first time from the manuscripts, the whole of the Rig-Veda with the great commentary of Sayana. He is a poor young man with an enormous design.

segments.name: Berlin and Paris — Bopp, Schelling, and the Vow before Burnouf

stops.name: Berlin — Bopp's grammar and Schelling's philosophy, 1844
stops.campa: He goes to Berlin, where two masters sit. From Franz Bopp, founder of comparative grammar, he learns how Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, German and Persian are branches of one root — the great discovery that a single family of speech, the Indo-European, runs from the Ganges to the Rhine. From the old Schelling he takes the yearning to read myth as revelation, and begins, at the philosopher's urging, a translation of the Upanishads. Here the two vocations of his life are joined: the science of language, exact and philological, and the science of religion, reverent and universal. Both begin in Berlin.

stops.name: Paris — Eugène Burnouf and the resolve to edit the Rig-Veda, 1845
stops.campa: In the spring of 1845 he comes to Paris and sits at the feet of Eugène Burnouf at the Collège de France, the first true master of the Veda and the Avesta in Europe. Burnouf lays the hymns before his pupils and says the great edition is still to be made — from the manuscripts, with Sayana's commentary, and it must be made in England, where the East India Company keeps the copies. To Max Müller this is a summons. Poor, foreign, and young, he takes the vow that will shape his whole existence: he will be the man who prints the oldest book of the Aryan world.
suggested_refs: Eugène Burnouf, Collège de France chair

stops.name: Paris — copying and collating manuscripts of the Veda
stops.campa: Through the year he labours in the libraries of Paris, copying and collating by hand the hymns and Sayana's vast gloss, letter by letter, verse by verse. There is no printed text to correct against; there is only the tangle of copies, each with its errors, from which the true reading must be reconstructed. It is the exact discipline of the poor Leipzig scholar now turned upon the sacred word. But the fullest manuscripts are not in Paris — they lie in London, in the Company's house. To finish what Burnouf has set him, he must cross the Channel.

segments.name: London and the Company — Bunsen and the Great Commission

stops.name: London — landfall, June 1846, and Baron Bunsen
stops.campa: In June 1846 he crosses to London with a letter to Baron Bunsen, the Prussian minister, who becomes his patron and intimate friend. Through Bunsen he is brought before Prince Albert and made known to Queen Victoria and the royal house; the poor young scholar finds himself at the Prussian embassy among crowned heads. Bunsen, a scholar-diplomat who dreams of tracing all mankind's languages to their fountainhead, sees in this exact young Vedist the instrument of his own vision. Together they will lay siege to the East India Company for the money to print the Veda.

stops.name: East India House, Leadenhall Street — the commission to print the Veda
stops.campa: Bunsen and Horace Hayman Wilson lay Müller's plan before the Court of Directors of the East India Company, and the Company undertakes to bear the cost of the edition — the printing of the Rig-Veda with Sayana's commentary, at the Company's charge. It is a strange and fated bargain: the great trading power that rules India will pay a German youth to print India's oldest scripture in England. The Company's own presses and manuscripts are opened to him. The commission is given. Max Müller has his life's work in his hands, and the first volume already forming.
suggested_refs: East India House, Leadenhall Street, engraving

stops.name: London — the poet's son writes a novel: Deutsche Liebe
stops.campa: The scholar of the Veda has another, softer gift, inherited from the poet of Dessau. In these years he writes Deutsche Liebe — German Love, a slight, tender tale of a doomed and spiritual love, published anonymously and beloved across Germany and England for generations. The hymns of the Brahmans he prints by day; by lamplight the son of Wilhelm Müller lets the old Romantic blood speak in his own soft German prose. It is his one work of the heart alone, and its readers never guess the same hand is toiling over Sayana's commentary. The two inheritances, the poet's and the philologist's, run side by side.
stops.quote: None but the lonely heart can know what I suffer... To love is to live, and to live is to love.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Deutsche Liebe / Memories: A Story of German Love (1857)
suggested_refs: Memories: A Story of German Love, English translation

segments.name: Oxford — The Edition and the New Sciences

stops.name: Oxford — the move to the University Press and 7 Norham Gardens
stops.campa: In the spring of 1848, the year of revolutions across Europe, Max Müller moves to Oxford to be near the University Press, which will print his Veda. He takes rooms, and in time the house at 7 Norham Gardens, north of the old walls, that will be his home until he dies — fifty-two years in a single English town. The German exile becomes an Oxford institution. From this quiet street of red brick and gardens, the hymns of the Ganges will issue volume by volume, and the whole enterprise of comparing the world's languages and the world's religions will find its centre.

stops.name: Oxford, Clarendon Press — the first volume of the Rig-Veda, 1849
stops.campa: The first volume of the Rig-Veda-Sanhita, the Sacred Hymns of the Brahmans, together with Sayana's commentary, comes from the Oxford press. For the first time the oldest book of the Aryan race stands printed and legible before the West, edited from the manuscripts by a man of five-and-twenty. Five more folio volumes will follow over the next quarter-century, the last in 1874. It is the labour of a lifetime begun at its threshold — the recovered scripture that Burnouf pointed to and the Company paid for, now a monument of German patience and English gold on an Oxford shelf.

stops.name: Oxford — Taylorian professor of modern European languages, 1850
stops.campa: He is appointed deputy Taylorian professor of modern European languages, and in 1854 full professor, at the Taylor Institution on St Giles'. He stocks its shelves with the German books he loves, Luther among them, and lectures on the tongues of living Europe even as he prints the dead tongue of the Veda. In 1851 he is made an honorary Master of Arts and a member of Christ Church; the foreigner is being woven into the fabric of Oxford. Here he begins to teach that all the languages of Europe and Asia are cousins, and that to compare them is a true science.

stops.name: Oxford, All Souls College — the life fellowship, 1858
stops.campa: In 1858 he is elected to a life fellowship at All Souls' College, the college without students, given over wholly to learning — a fitting cloister for a man whose students are the dead hymnodists of India. The next year, having become a British subject in 1855, he marries Georgina Grenfell, overcoming the long resistance of both families. The German poet's son is now an English gentleman, a Fellow of All Souls, householder of Norham Gardens, married into the English gentry. His roots in Oxford are set for good; only his books will keep travelling east.

stops.name: Oxford — the loss of the Boden Chair of Sanskrit, 1860
stops.campa: The Boden Professorship of Sanskrit falls vacant, the great prize of his field, and Max Müller stands for it against Monier Monier-Williams. Convocation votes — and the wider, less learned electorate defeats him. He is the finest Sanskritist in Europe and he is passed over, because he is foreign, because the Boden chair was founded to convert India and the electors fear his sympathy for the old religion. He writes to his mother that all the best people voted for him, the professors almost to a man, but the vulgus profanum made the majority. It is the wound of his life.
stops.quote: All the best people voted for me, the Professors almost unanimously, but the vulgus profanum made the majority.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, letter to his mother (1860), in Life and Letters

stops.name: Oxford — Lectures on the Science of Language, 1861-1864
stops.campa: At the Royal Institution he delivers the Lectures on the Science of Language, which make him famous throughout the English-speaking world. Language, he teaches, is not a human invention but a growth with its own laws, a natural object to be studied like the stars — a true science. In these lectures falls the sentence for which he is longest remembered: that mythology is a disease of language, a fever that seizes words when their first, plain meaning is forgotten and their names harden into gods. From this seed his whole reading of myth will grow.
stops.quote: Mythology is in truth a disease of language. A myth means a word, but a word which, from being a name or an attribute, has been allowed to assume a more substantial existence.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Lectures on the Science of Language, Second Series (1864)
suggested_refs: Lectures on the Science of Language, 1861 edition

stops.name: Oxford — Chips from a German Workshop, 1867
stops.campa: He gathers his scattered essays into a series he wryly names Chips from a German Workshop — the shavings, he says, that fall from the bench of a German craftsman at work in England. In them he ranges over comparative mythology, the Vedas, Buddhism, the songs of his homeland, the life of Schiller, the memory of his own father. Through these volumes the English reading public learns to think of religion and language as things that can be compared across all the earth. The workshop is his mind; the chips are the essays; and by them the new sciences spread far beyond the lecture-room into the parlours of the age.
suggested_refs: Chips from a German Workshop, 4 vols.

segments.name: The Solar Myth and the Sacred Books — the World's Scriptures Englished

stops.name: Oxford — Comparative Mythology and the solar-myth theory
stops.campa: In his essay on Comparative Mythology and the lectures that follow, Max Müller unfolds the doctrine that all the gods are the dawn and the sun. The first men, he teaches, had no abstractions; they spoke of the sunrise as a bright maiden fleeing before her pursuer, of the sun as a hero who slays the night. When the plain words were forgotten, the phrases were mistaken for persons, and out of the daily miracle of daybreak grew Apollo and Daphne and the whole shining company. Nomina became numina: the names became the powers. Every dawn, he says, the oldest religion of the world is re-enacted in the sky.
stops.quote: The whole theogony and philosophy of the ancient world centred in the Dawn, the mother of the bright gods, the mother of the morning.

stops.name: Oxford — first Professor of Comparative Philology, 1868
stops.campa: The University creates for him, and for him alone, a Chair of Comparative Philology — the first in Oxford — which he holds to his death. The defeat over the Boden chair is answered: a new science is founded with him at its head. From this chair he governs the comparison of the Indo-European tongues and the reconstruction of the common Aryan speech and home from which, he holds, the fathers of Greek and Roman and German and Indian all set out. The exile who could not have the old chair is given a new one, cut to the shape of his own mind.

stops.name: Westminster Abbey — Introduction to the Science of Religion, 1870
stops.campa: At the Royal Institution and before great audiences he founds a second science: the Science of Religion, the comparative study of all the faiths of mankind, weighed one against another without partiality. He gives it its watchword, borrowed from Goethe on languages: he who knows one, knows none. To know a single religion, even one's own, is not to understand religion at all; only by laying the scriptures of the world side by side can their common truth be seen. He is called, and calls himself, the founder of the science of religion — the study of God made a study of comparison.
stops.quote: He who knows one, knows none.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Introduction to the Science of Religion (1873)
suggested_refs: Introduction to the Science of Religion, 1873

stops.name: Oxford — the Veda completed: six folios closed, 1874
stops.campa: In 1874 the sixth and last folio of the Rig-Veda with Sayana's commentary leaves the press, and the labour Burnouf set him in Paris a generation before is finished. Twenty-five years of copying, collating, and correcting are bound and done; the oldest book of the Aryan world stands complete in print, edited whole for the first time in history. He is fifty, honoured across Europe, the acknowledged prince of Sanskrit learning though the Boden chair was never his. The young man's impossible design is a shelf of great books. On this foundation the science of language he founded at Oxford will pass to abler grammarians after him.

stops.name: Westminster, Chapter House — the Hibbert Lectures, 1878
stops.campa: In the Chapter House of Westminster Abbey he delivers the first Hibbert Lectures, On the Origin and Growth of Religion as Illustrated by the Religions of India. Under the vaults of the English abbey the man who edited the Veda expounds to a Christian audience how the hymns of the Ganges first reached out toward the Infinite through the perception of the sun and dawn and sky. He argues that behind all the idols and rites lies a genuine intimation of the divine, older than any creed. The comparison of religions is now preached in the very heart of English Christendom, and heard.
stops.quote: There is a monotheism that precedes the polytheism of the Veda; and even in the invocations of their innumerable gods the remembrance of a God, one and infinite, breaks through the mist of an idolatrous phraseology.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Hibbert Lectures on the Origin and Growth of Religion (1878)

stops.name: Oxford — the Sacred Books of the East begun, 1879
stops.campa: Now comes the crown of his labour. From the Clarendon Press he begins the Sacred Books of the East, a great series in which the scriptures of the non-Christian world are to be Englished by the best hands in Europe and set before the West — the Vedas and Upanishads, the Buddhist and Jain canons, the laws of Manu, the sayings of Confucius and Lao-tzu, the Qur'an, the books of the Zoroastrians. He is general editor of all fifty volumes. It is the first time the holy books of Asia are gathered and translated as one library. The comparison he preaches is now a shelf a man can hold.
stops.quote: The translations of the Sacred Books of the East... are intended to make people acquainted with the foundations of the great religions of the East.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Preface to the Sacred Books of the East (1879)
suggested_refs: Sacred Books of the East, 50-volume set
Upanishads, SBE vols. I and XV

stops.name: Oxford — the Avesta given to the West: Müller faces Zoroaster
stops.campa: Among the fifty volumes he sets the Zend-Avesta, the scripture of Zarathustra the Prophet, given in three parts by James Darmesteter and L. H. Mills. Across the centuries Max Müller the editor and Zoroaster the seer face one another: the Persian who taught the war of Light against the Lie, and the German who gathers his hymns into the same library as the Veda and the Gospel. In the Gathas of the prophet the Wise Lord Ahura Mazda speaks; through Müller's series the fire-altar's oldest liturgy is carried, in English, to readers who never smelt its smoke. The Prophet's word joins the shelf of the world's scriptures.
stops.quote: As long as man continues to be man, he will always long to know something of the Beyond, of the Infinite, of the Divine.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East, general preface
suggested_refs: Zend-Avesta, Sacred Books of the East vols. IV, XXIII, XXXI

stops.name: Glasgow — the Gifford Lectures on Natural Religion, 1888-1892
stops.campa: Called to Glasgow as Gifford Lecturer, he gives across four years four great courses on natural religion, physical religion, anthropological religion, and last the theosophy or psychological religion in which the human soul reaches toward the divine. It is the summing-up of his life's thought: that religion, like language, is a natural growth in man, universal, comparable, and everywhere reaching for the Infinite that lies beyond sense. The old scholar, honoured throughout Europe, stands in the Scottish university and offers, as his final testament, a science of the sacred embracing all the faiths whose books he has spent his years translating.
stops.quote: Religion is a mental faculty which, independent of, nay in spite of sense and reason, enables man to apprehend the Infinite under different names and under varying disguises.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Natural Religion (Gifford Lectures, 1889)

segments.name: The Aryan Word — Its Sin, Its Repudiation, Its Abusers

stops.name: Oxford — the Aryan hypothesis: one home, one speech
stops.campa: From his chair Max Müller teaches the great genealogy: that Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Celtic, German and Persian spring from one lost mother-tongue, and that the peoples who spoke it once dwelt together in a single home before scattering. He calls them the Aryas, the Aryans, after the name the Veda gives its noble folk. The word is a name for a family of speech; in his mouth an argument for kinship, proof that Brahman and Englishman are cousins from one hearth. His method passes to abler heirs, among them the Oxford philologist Tolkien, who from the same comparative science invents whole tongues and a mythology to house them.
stops.quote: There is an unbroken continuity between the most modern and the most ancient thoughts of mankind... We are the Aryas, and we come from the East.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Lectures on the Science of Language (1861)

stops.name: Oxford — the repudiation: 'a great sinner,' 1888
stops.campa: He lives to see his philologist's word poisoned. Others take 'Aryan,' which he coined for a family of speech, and make of it a family of blood — Aryan skulls, Aryan eyes, a master race. In Biographies of Words and the Home of the Aryas he denounces them without mercy: to speak of an Aryan race, Aryan blood, Aryan eyes and hair, he writes, is as gross a blunder as to speak of a long-skulled grammar. Language is no measure of race. The very kinship he proved, he argues, is the strongest weapon against those who would divide mankind by blood. He forespoke the word and disowns its abuse.
stops.quote: To me an ethnologist who speaks of Aryan race, Aryan blood, Aryan eyes and hair, is as great a sinner as a linguist who speaks of a dolichocephalic dictionary or a brachycephalic grammar.
stops.quote_source: F. Max Müller, Biographies of Words and the Home of the Aryas (1888)
suggested_refs: Biographies of Words and the Home of the Aryas, 1888

stops.name: Beyond Oxford — the abusers he foreran and disowned
stops.campa: Yet the word runs on past him into darkness he did not choose. After his death the racial reading he condemned is seized by mythographers of the coming century — by Savitri Devi, who will make of the Aryan an Aryan god-race and of Hitler an avatar of Vishnu; by Miguel Serrano, who will forge from the same word an esoteric Hitlerism of blood and light. They stand at the far, disfigured end of a road whose first stone he laid and whose direction he damned. Max Müller forespoke their vocabulary and repudiated their meaning; the sin he named as sin, they raised as a banner.
suggested_refs: Savitri Devi, The Lightning and the Sun

segments.name: The Friends of the End — Vivekananda, the Empress, and Holywell

stops.name: Oxford — the friendship of the crowned: the Empress Frederick
stops.campa: The poor scholar of Leipzig has become the friend of thrones. Through Bunsen he had come to Queen Victoria and Prince Albert; now for decades he corresponds with Victoria, Princess Royal — the Empress Frederick, mother of the German Kaiser — who confides in the great Anglo-German savant her hopes and griefs from Berlin. His letters pass between Oxford and the Prussian court; he is honoured with the Prussian Pour le Mérite and made a Privy Councillor of the British crown. The exile who fled the revolutions of 1848 sits at last in the confidence of the very houses that ruled the century.
suggested_refs: Pour le Mérite, civil class medal

stops.name: Oxford, 7 Norham Gardens — Vivekananda at luncheon, 28 May 1896
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of May, Swami Vivekananda, disciple of the God-man Ramakrishna, comes to luncheon at Norham Gardens. The aged philologist and the young monk of Calcutta sit together, and Müller shows his guest the proofs of an essay he is writing — 'A Real Mahatman,' his portrait of Ramakrishna, which will appear in August and give the saint of Dakshineswar his first fame in the West. Vivekananda departs marvelling that the great Western scholar of the Veda is at heart a Vedantist, and writes that Müller may yet carry his master's message to the world. East and West break bread in the old man's garden.
stops.quote: I wish to see you before I die. So Sri Ramakrishna's message has reached even here.
stops.quote_source: reported of Max Müller by Swami Vivekananda, Brahmavadin (6 June 1896)
suggested_refs: 'A Real Mahatman,' The Nineteenth Century, Aug. 1896

stops.name: Oxford — Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, 1898
stops.campa: The essay grows into a book: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, in which the founder of the science of religion, near the end of his own days, offers the West a living Indian saint and not merely an ancient text. The man who taught that all the gods are the dawn, and that he who knows one religion knows none, closes his career by pointing not to a hymn but to a person — a Bengali mystic of his own century as evidence that the East still breeds the holy. The comparison of scriptures ends in reverence for a man; the Vedist becomes, half, a Vedantist.

stops.name: Oxford, 7 Norham Gardens — the death, 28 October 1900
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of October, in the house at Norham Gardens where he has lived for two-and-fifty years, Friedrich Max Müller dies at seventy-six. On his deathbed he dictates to his son the last corrections to his autobiography, which he leaves a fragment, carried only to his early Oxford days — as if the man who edited so many ancient books could not finish the editing of his own life. The Veda is printed, the fifty Sacred Books stand on the shelf, the two sciences are founded. The poet's son from the enchanted island of Dessau lays down the pen he held with the only fortune he ever had.

stops.name: Oxford, Holywell Cemetery — the granite Celtic cross, 1 November 1900
stops.campa: On the first of November he is buried in Holywell Cemetery, under a great Celtic cross of granite — a Western, Christian sign over the man who gave the West the scriptures of the East. Around him lie the Oxford dead among the wild flowers of the old ground. A memorial fund is raised for Indian studies; in a later age the German cultural houses of India will bear his name, and a street in Delhi be called for him. The stranger who arrived a stranger, as his father's song had it, is laid to rest at home at last, cousin to the Aryas he spent his life reading.
suggested_refs: Max Müller's Celtic cross, Holywell Cemetery
